According to the Defender of Rights 2020 report, biased data can contribute to algorithmic discrimination by reflecting past discriminatory practices and systemic discrimination present in society. When algorithms are trained on such biased data, they can reproduce and even exacerbate existing biases. 

On the other hand, apparently neutral criteria can also lead to discriminatory effects. These criteria may not directly include prohibited grounds for discrimination, but their combination can correlate with protected characteristics, resulting in similar discriminatory outcomes. For example, using seemingly neutral criteria like the institution of origin in university algorithms can indirectly discriminate against youths of foreign origin due to existing residential and educational segregation. Thus, both biased data and neutral criteria can create conditions for discrimination through the mechanisms of algorithms.
